zone: Ptarmigan crest between Cache Col and White Rock Lakes
_areas_note: The peaks on the middle third of the Ptarmigan crest, reached by driving the Cascade River Road to its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead, walking the maintained trail to the pass, then turning south over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col onto the traverse. Cache Col is the southern boundary of North Cascades National Park, so every peak in this list sits in Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest ground and needs only a free self-issue wilderness permit; the nights spent north of the col, at the pass or on the Cache Glacier shoulder, are the ones that need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at Marblemount. Mount Formidable also has a second, entirely separate approach on the same road: the South Fork Cascade River trailhead at a bend around mile 17-18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, with a climbers' line up Drop Creek that avoids glacier travel altogether, and two of the sites below belong to it rather than to the traverse. NOTHING FROM THE TWO NEIGHBOURING FILES IS REPEATED. The Cascade River Road file covers Boston Basin, Sahale Glacier Camp, Pelton Basin and Johannesburg Camp, all north of Cache Col inside the park. The Ptarmigan crest and Gunsight file covers Kool-Aid Lake, Yang Yang Lakes, White Rock Lakes, Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake, the Bachelor Creek camps, Spire Col and the Dome Glacier cols. Those eleven sites are the established stops on this crest and none of them appear here; what follows is the ground between them, which is where parties actually sleep when they are climbing a peak rather than walking through. TWO PEAKS WERE REMOVED. Trapper Mountain drains into Trapper Lake and tributaries of the Stehekin River and sits on the park and wilderness boundary southeast of Cascade Pass, with its nearest higher neighbour under a mile away being Hurry-up Peak; it is a Horseshoe Basin objective looked at from the Black Warrior Mine side of Basin Creek, not a traverse peak, and it belongs with the Horseshoe Basin camps at Basin Creek and Cottonwood. Rimrock Ridge is in Chelan County on the Agnes Mountain quadrangle, east of the crest in the Flat Creek and Agnes Creek drainage that runs to the Stehekin; no traverse account mentions it, and its practical access is the Flat Creek trail out of the upper Stehekin valley rather than anything reached by turning south at Cascade Pass. Both ids are omitted. Elephant Head is kept but is the weakest fit: it sits at the far south end of this stretch, immediately above White Rock Lakes on the divide toward the Chickamin and the west fork of Agnes Creek, and a party coming north over Dome Peak from Downey Creek reaches it about as easily as one coming south from Cascade Pass.

sites.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
sites.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.
sites.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
sites.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
sites.notes: The col is the gateway to everything in this file. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.

sites.name: Spider-Formidable Col
sites.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.
sites.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
sites.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Published elevations for the col disagree badly, with figures from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet, so no number is recorded here rather than pick one. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.

sites.name: Drop Creek high camp
sites.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.
sites.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
sites.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.

sites.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps
sites.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.
sites.water: The South Fork and Drop Creek itself, running all season. Water is never the problem down here; the log crossing in high water can be.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
sites.notes: The fallback first night on the Drop Creek approach to Formidable, for a party that starts late or is not confident of reaching the high camp in one push. It exists because the valley section is slower than its mileage suggests once the maintained tread runs out, with overgrown stretches and repeated small gains and losses. Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. No elevation is given because no confident figure was found for the usual sites.

sites.name: Le Conte Pass
sites.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.
sites.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
sites.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.

sites.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
sites.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.
sites.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
sites.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. Sources disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.

sites.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
sites.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.
sites.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
sites.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak in this file, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else in the file: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
